about: CHAIN barrow (Design/content/chains/barrow.md): a broken burial mound on the hoe above the Deben (Sutton Hoo), 793 to about 813. Thirteen cards. A fowler at Gipeswic tells of gold showing in a mound the gale has broken, beside the gallows the king's reeve keeps among the old kings; the boat lands; the four men of the crew (the spine's Aldger, Ravn, Brunger and Beornwine) each want a different thing done with a dead heathen's gold; a fever follows; a goldsmith at Dorestad knows old work; an old woman of the old kings' kin says who lies there (Raedwald of the two altars, Bede II.15, if it is he); the reeve hangs a potter's lad and asks after boats; and on a second night the great ship mound lies whole beside the broken one. Four endings: back into the earth (what really happened: the ship mound lay whole until 1939; the hard road), the bishop at Dommoc (Gregory's letter to Mellitus, Bede I.30), the king's reeve (the finder's share), and the goldsmith's crucible. To open the great mound is history changed: flag changed_sutton_hoo_opened. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Every *_key has its words in Data/writing/chain_barrow.json; an option's outcome key is named in its note. (?) marks what could not be checked.

cards.note: Step 1, the start (drawn at Gipeswic from 793 to 811). A fowler of the Deben tells of the hoe: the mounds of the old kings above the river, the gallows the reeve keeps there, and a mound a gale has broken. The place is Sutton Hoo: about twenty mounds on a spur ('hoo', a hill shaped like a heel spur) over the tidal Deben, 11 km from the sea; a gallows stood on Mound 5 and executed people were buried round it from the 8th and 9th centuries onwards (Wikipedia 'Sutton Hoo', read 6 Oct 2026; Carver's excavations). The broken mound is ours: most of the mounds were robbed at dates nobody knows. King Aethelberht's penny with the she-wolf and twins: dossiers/gipeswic.md. He was beheaded at Offa's order in 794 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 792). The gallows line is the warning for steps 2, 7 and 8. Sets ch_barrow_1; ch_barrow_way if he is paid.

cards.note: Step 2 (a sea card, drawn soon after she sails once step 1 is done: the Deben is the next river north of the Orwell). The landing under the hoe and the broken mound. The gold mount is modelled on the gold and garnet belt and sword fittings of Sutton Hoo Mounds 1 and 17 (stepped garnets in cells over stamped foil); the bronze bowl with burnt bone is as the cremations in bronze bowls of Mounds 5 to 7 (Carver; from memory (?)). The shifting bar of the Deben is real. A failed dig is seen from the far bank (ch_barrow_seen), which the reeve uses in step 7; the gallows in step 1 was the warning. Sets ch_barrow_2 and ch_barrow_piece (the gold aboard) or ch_barrow_clean (nothing touched).

cards.note: Step 3 (a crew card, the night after the landing). The four men of the spine's crew each have a reason. Aldger: gold is made clean by the church. Ravn: the dead keep what they were given; the ship mound at Ogvaldsnes is Storhaug on Karmoy, a ship burial dated 779 (from memory (?)); that a mound's dweller walks after a robber is the belief of the later sagas, set back here (?). Brunger: the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 22 (c. 782-785) orders the bodies of Christian Saxons carried to the church's cemeteries and not to the mounds of the pagans (MGH Capit. I no. 26). Beornwine: Felix's Life of Guthlac (730-740, written for King Aelfwald of the East Angles) says Guthlac's mound at Crowland had been dug open by greedy men hoping for treasure (c. 28; Wikipedia 'Guthlac of Crowland', read 6 Oct 2026); and the dragon's hoard and the stolen cup are Beowulf, fitt XXXII (texts_793.json beowulf_32). Nothing is quoted. Sets ch_barrow_3, a six-day timer ch_barrow_ague, and ch_barrow_vow_church or ch_barrow_vow_back if a word is given.

cards.note: Step 4 (a crew card, six days or more after the quarrel). The Saxon has the shaking sickness of the marshes, which comes every third day: the spring sickness (lencten adl) of the Old English leechbooks (?); the fens' sickness is in Felix's Guthlac. The men blame the mound. A cut penny given to the water is a heathen offering as the old_gods chain has them; fasting, prayer and the sign of the cross are the church's answer. No option harms: the fever passes on the third day whatever is done, and the men credit what was done. Sets ch_barrow_4 and ch_barrow_rite_old or ch_barrow_rite_new.

cards.note: Step 5 (drawn at Dorestad once the fever is past). Folcmar the goldsmith (invented) knows old English work when he sees it. Garnet cloisonné over stamped gold foil is the work of the 6th and 7th centuries; it stops when the garnets stop coming, about the middle of the 7th century (the usual account; (?)). Gold to silver at one for twelve is the Carolingian reckoning (the Edict of Pitres, 864, c. 24, fixes it; earlier by custom (?)). The mount, about 18 g of gold, is 160 d: the chain's first turn payout. The riddles are the Exeter Book's on ore or gold (riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_83_ore, Tupper 1910) and Gestumblindi's on the goldsmith's hammer (r-gest-04). Sets ch_barrow_5 and a timer ch_barrow_rest of 45 days; ch_barrow_piece_sold if it is melted; ch_barrow_buyer if he is asked about a whole grave.

cards.note: Step 6 (drawn at Gipeswic or Dommoc, 45 days or more after the goldsmith). Leofwaru (invented), an old woman of the old kings' kin by the distaff side, says who lies on the hoe. Raedwald, king of the East Angles, was baptised in Kent and at home kept in one temple an altar for Christ and a small one for offerings to devils; King Aldwulf saw that temple as a boy (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica II.15). That the great ship mound is his has been the likeliest reading since 1940 and is still disputed (Wikipedia 'Sutton Hoo'): she says so. The kings' names are Bede's and the Anglian collection's: Wuffa, Tytila, Raedwald, Eorpwald, Anna, Aelfwald (d. 749), after whom the line is lost. Aethelberht was killed at Offa's order in 794; Offa died in July 796; Eadwald struck coin as king of the East Angles from about 796 and Coenwulf of Mercia had the kingdom again by about 798 to 805 (Wikipedia 'Eadwald of East Anglia', read 6 Oct 2026). Her last line is the warning for steps 7 and 8. Sets ch_barrow_6 and a timer ch_barrow_winter of 60 days; ch_barrow_kin_known if she is told.

cards.note: Step 7 (drawn at Gipeswic in the sailing months, 60 days or more after step 6). The reeve has hanged a potter's lad, Dudda (invented; Gipeswic is the town of the Ipswich-ware potters), who dug in the broken mound by daylight; the gallows on the hoe is the one of step 1. That treasure found in the earth is the king's is written down only in the 12th century (Leges Henrici Primi 10.1, 'thesaurus inventus' among the king's rights); a finder's share by custom is ours (?). The kings by year are as in step 6. To deny is a chance: if it fails the house pays 40 d and the hoe is watched (ch_barrow_watched). Sets ch_barrow_7; ch_barrow_reeve_knows if he is told; ch_barrow_church_named if the bishop is named.

cards.note: Step 8 (a sea card, drawn soon after she sails from Gipeswic once the reeve has asked). The second landing, at night. The great mound at the river end is Sutton Hoo Mound 1: a ship 27 m long with a chamber amidships, and in it the helm, the sword with gold and garnet at the hilt, the great gold buckle, a purse of thirty-seven small gold coins, silver dishes with the stamps of the emperor Anastasius, and more (Wikipedia 'Sutton Hoo'). It lay whole until 1939. To open it is the chain's change of history: a success sets ch_barrow_great and changed_sutton_hoo_opened. A failure leaves a pit that missed the chamber, as the robbers' pit of the 16th century really did, and the small mound's leavings aboard (ch_barrow_hoard). The small mound's goods (a blue glass cup, buckles, gold from a sword, a pouch lid) are as what robbers left in Mound 2 and what lay in Mound 17 (Wikipedia 'Sutton Hoo'). Laying turf back sets ch_barrow_closed. Sets ch_barrow_8.

cards.note: Step 9 (a crew card, drawn at sea after the second landing): where it goes. Each road schedules its own ending: back into the earth and word to the kin (30 days, Gipeswic), the bishop (20 days, Dommoc), the king's reeve (30 days, Gipeswic), or the goldsmith's crucible (25 days, Dorestad). A man who opened the great mound cannot put it back past a watch (the first choice is closed to him); a man with only the one piece or nothing has nothing a goldsmith would open his door for (the last is closed to him). The lines about a word given are the vows of step 3. Sets ch_barrow_9 and one of ch_barrow_to_earth, ch_barrow_to_church, ch_barrow_to_king, ch_barrow_to_sale.

cards.note: ENDING 'earth' (scheduled 30 days after step 9, at Gipeswic): what really happened, and the hard road. The great ship mound lay whole until 1939, and the gold of it stayed in the ground for thirteen hundred years. The old kings' kin pay in what such a family has: a toft on the Orwell bank (Gipeswic's plots ran down to the river; wells lined with old wine casks are found there: dossiers/gipeswic.md), wool rents in the coin of three kings, a ring of her own. Handing over land with a turf from it before witnesses is the later custom, set back here (?). The fowler's gift is the knowledge of the Deben bar. Sets ch_barrow_end_earth and two grand rewards: unlock_pilot_deben with unlock_plot_gipeswic or unlock_heirloom_wuffing_ring.

cards.note: ENDING 'church' (scheduled 20 days after step 9, at Dommoc, the East Angles' bishop's seat since Felix, c. 630). The bishop's first line is Pope Gregory's letter to Mellitus of 601: the temples of the English are not to be pulled down, but the idols cast out, holy water sprinkled and altars set up (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica I.30); it is retold, not quoted. Raedwald's baptism in Kent: Bede II.15. Botolph began his minster at Icanho (Iken on the Alde) in 654 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 654); a cloth laid on a saint's tomb is the commonest relic of the age. The bishop's letter for the boat is modelled on the churches' own toll-free ships (the charters of King Aethelbald for London, 730s and 740s (?)). The cross on the hoe is ours; the gallows there in fact went on into the 11th century, so with it the place's history is changed a little. With the great mound's goods the king's gear becomes church plate (changed_sutton_hoo_opened was set in step 8). Sets ch_barrow_end_church; grand rewards unlock_title_st_felix_man, and with a hoard unlock_relic_st_botolph_cloth, and with the great hoard unlock_work_gipeswic_hoe_cross.

cards.note: ENDING 'king' (scheduled 30 days after step 9, at Gipeswic). The reeve pays the finder before the town. A third to the finder is ours (?). The king's leaf is modelled on King Aethelbald's remissions of the toll on one ship at the port of London to Rochester, Minster-in-Thanet and the bishop of London (Sawyer 86, 87, 88, 91, 98, 1788; 730s and 740s; from memory (?)): Latin on parchment, with the king's cross and his witnesses' crosses, and no seal. Such a grant to a foreign layman is the game's. The king by year is as in step 6: before 794 the gold stays with the East Angles' own king, and the year after he is dead and it is Offa's; from 794 it goes to Mercia. With the great mound's goods a king's regalia is broken up among another king's men (changed_sutton_hoo_opened). The lasting cost is the old kin's enmity (ch_barrow_kin_enmity). Sets ch_barrow_end_king; grand reward unlock_charter_gipeswic, and with the great hoard unlock_title_kings_merchant_gipeswic.

cards.note: ENDING 'sold' (scheduled 25 days after step 9, at Dorestad). The crucible. Gold for silver at one to twelve, less the goldsmith's fire and silence. With the small mound's goods this is only what happened to most of the hoe's mounds, by hands nobody recorded. With the great mound's it is the chain's largest change of history: the helm, the buckle and the Greek silver of Sutton Hoo Mound 1 are melted at Dorestad or scattered, and the men of 1939 find an empty ship (changed_sutton_hoo_opened, set in step 8). The dishes' stamps are the emperor Anastasius's (491-518). The helm is iron with tinned bronze, silver wire and garnets (Wikipedia 'Sutton Hoo helmet', from memory (?)). The lasting costs: a mound-breaker's name (ch_barrow_mound_breaker), and with the great hoard the Northman leaves the boat (ch_barrow_ravn_gone: for the spine to act on). Sets ch_barrow_end_sold; grand reward unlock_heirloom_garnet_pommel, unlock_heirloom_old_kings_helm, or unlock_ship_north_sea_merchant_ship (a place on the slip, not the hull).
